title: The Exponential Distribution
quickIdea: The waiting time until the next event of a Poisson process is exponential: density lambda e^(-lambda x), survival e^(-lambda x), mean 1/lambda, and it forgets how long you have already waited.
remember: Density f(x) = lambda e^(-lambda x) for x >= 0 and 0 for x < 0; CDF F(x) = 1 - e^(-lambda x); survival P(X > x) = e^(-lambda x).
Mean 1/lambda and variance 1/lambda^2, so the standard deviation equals the mean - a property unique to this family among the ones GATE asks about.
lambda is a rate, not a mean. 'Mean lifetime 10 years' means lambda = 0.1 per year, and the density is 0.1 e^(-0.1 x).
Memorylessness: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). The conditional probability of waiting t more is the same as the unconditional one, however long you have already waited.
For every lambda, P(X > mean) = e^(-1) = 0.3679. This is why the 2021 question does not need the value of lambda at all.
The median is (ln 2)/lambda, which is less than the mean 1/lambda - the distribution is right-skewed, so the median sits below the mean.

example.prompt: The lifetime of a component is exponential with parameter 2. What is the probability that its lifetime exceeds its expected lifetime?
example.work: The expected lifetime is 1/lambda = 1/2. So the question is P(X > 1/2) = e^(-2 x 1/2) = e^(-1). Numerically e^(-1) = 0.367879.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2021 Set 1 Q.18 is this question, and the point of it is that the answer does not depend on lambda: P(X > 1/lambda) = e^(-lambda/lambda) = e^(-1) for every rate. Any option that needs the number 2 has been computed along a longer route than necessary.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2021 Set 1 Q.18: the lifetime of a component is exponentially distributed with parameter 2. The probability that its lifetime exceeds the expected lifetime (two decimal places) is ______.
variations.why: The mean is 1/2, so P(X > 1/2) = e^(-2 x 1/2) = e^(-1). The accepted range is 0.36 to 0.37, which is the rounding of 0.3679.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A telephone call lasts on average 4 minutes, exponentially distributed. Find the probability that a call lasts more than 6 minutes, and the probability that it lasts more than 10 minutes given that it has already lasted 6.
variations.why: lambda = 1/4 per minute, so P(X > 6) = e^(-6/4). The conditional question is memorylessness: having waited 6 minutes leaves the same distribution of remaining time, so the answer is P(X > 4) and not the unconditional P(X > 10) = 0.0821.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A used laptop has lasted 3 years. Its lifetime is exponential with mean 4 years. Is it more likely to fail in the next year than a new one?
variations.answer: No - exactly as likely, by memorylessness.
variations.why: P(X > 4 | X > 3) = P(X > 1) = e^(-0.25) = 0.7788 for both. This is the property that makes the exponential unsuitable for modelling wear-out, and it is the property GATE tests when it says 'exponential'.

trap.what: Treating the parameter as the mean, or applying the memoryless rule when the distribution is not exponential.
trap.why: For the exponential, lambda is the rate; the mean is 1/lambda. And memorylessness is a special property, not a general one: a uniform variable on (0, 10) that has survived 5 units is certainly about to fail within 5 more.
trap.counterexample: With 'mean 4 minutes' read as lambda = 4, P(X > 6) becomes e^(-24) = 3.8 x 10^(-11) instead of e^(-1.5) = 0.2231. For the uniform variable on (0, 10), P(X > 8 | X > 5) = 2/5 while P(X > 3) = 0.7 - memorylessness fails.

check.question: X is exponential with mean 4. Find P(X > 4), P(X <= 2) and the variance.
check.explanation: lambda = 1/4, so the survival at 4 is e^(-1) and the CDF at 2 is 1 - e^(-2/4). The variance is 1/lambda^2 = 16, so the standard deviation is 4, equal to the mean.
